description: Compare definitions of health, illness, disease and well-being and how they overlap.
hero_image_caption: A GP in consultation — health is more than the absence of disease.
content_html:
Why Definitions Matter

In health and social care, precise language is essential. The words “health”, “illness”, “disease” and “well-being” are used by practitioners every day — but they do not all mean the same thing. The exam unit requires you to know four specific definitions, each drawn from a named authoritative source. These definitions are not interchangeable, and mark schemes credit only candidates who can distinguish between them accurately. This lesson covers each definition in turn, explains its source, and explores the interpretive layers that the exam also assesses.

Health — The WHO Definition

The most widely used definition of health comes from the World Health Organization (WHO). The WHO defines health as “a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity.” This definition was established in 1948 and remains the standard reference point for practitioners and policymakers.

Three features of this definition are particularly important for the exam. First, it is holistic — it covers physical, mental and social dimensions, not just the physical body. Second, it goes beyond the absence of disease: a person may be free from identifiable illness but still not be healthy if their mental or social well-being is poor. Third, it uses the phrase “complete” well-being, which implies a high standard — a standard that some argue is rarely achievable in practice.

Key Fact

The WHO (1948) defines health as: “a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity.” The key phrase is not merely the absence of disease — health is a positive state, not just the lack of illness.

Illness — A Personal Experience

While the WHO definition of health is a professional, objective standard, illness is defined quite differently. Drawing on the British Medical Journal, the specification frames illness as the feeling or experience of ill health — a subjective state that is personal to the individual. This is a crucial distinction: illness is what a person feels, not what a test detects.

The significance of this definition is illustrated by two scenarios. First, illness without disease: a person may feel genuinely unwell — fatigued, in pain, anxious — but no physical cause can be found by medical tests. The person is experiencing illness even though no disease is present. Conditions such as medically unexplained symptoms, chronic fatigue syndrome or certain forms of chronic pain fall into this category. Second, the reverse is also possible: a person may have a diagnosed disease (for example, early-stage hypertension) but feel completely well in themselves. In that case, disease is present without the individual experiencing illness.

In a care setting, a practitioner who only acts when a medically confirmed disease is present may fail to support individuals experiencing genuine illness. A person who says they feel exhausted, anxious and unable to cope deserves to be taken seriously even if blood tests come back clear. Equally, a person with a confirmed chronic condition may not feel “ill” on a daily basis and may not want to be treated as unwell. Person-centred care requires practitioners to respond to both the objective condition and the subjective experience of health.

Disease — Signs and Symptoms

Disease is defined by the specification as a condition characterised by specific signs and symptoms. Unlike illness, which is subjective, disease is an objective, clinically identifiable state. Signs are what a practitioner can observe or measure — a rash, an elevated white blood cell count, a raised temperature. Symptoms are what the patient reports feeling — pain, breathlessness, nausea. A disease can typically be named (for example, pneumonia, type 2 diabetes, multiple sclerosis) and diagnosed through clinical assessment or testing.

It is important to remember that an individual can have a disease without experiencing illness (as in the early-stage hypertension example above), and can experience illness without having a diagnosable disease. Examiners test this distinction — knowing only the general meaning of each word is not enough. You need to be able to explain the specific conceptual difference and give an example that illustrates it.

Key Fact

Illness is the personal, subjective experience of feeling unwell — you can have illness without disease. Disease is an objective, clinically identified condition with specific signs and symptoms — you can have disease without experiencing illness. The two do not always go together.

Well-being — More Than Feeling Fine

The fourth definition — well-being — draws on Psychology Today’s definition. Well-being is described as being happy, healthy and thriving, with good mental health, high life satisfaction, a sense of purpose, and the ability to manage stress. Like the WHO definition of health, well-being is a broad, positive concept — it is about flourishing, not merely the absence of problems.

Well-being differs from health in that it places greater emphasis on the subjective sense of thriving. A person can be medically healthy in the WHO sense but still have low well-being if they feel their life lacks purpose or if they are chronically stressed. This distinction is relevant in care settings: practitioners promoting well-being are not just treating illness or disease — they are supporting individuals to flourish and find meaning.

A holistic view of health recognises that what it means to be “healthy” or to have “well-being” is not universal. These concepts vary between cultures (some cultures prioritise collective harmony over individual health; others integrate spiritual health into their understanding of well-being), across time (historical understandings of health were very different from today’s biomedical model — Victorian medicine did not recognise mental illness in the same way), and across life stages (a 3-year-old’s well-being is largely about attachment and play; a 75-year-old’s well-being may be more about autonomy, social connection and freedom from pain). Practitioners who appreciate this variation are better placed to provide genuinely person-centred care.
exam_tip_html: Mark schemes for questions on these four definitions often carry a source attribution requirement — candidates who name the WHO for health, the British Medical Journal for illness, and Psychology Today for well-being earn additional credit. Practise writing all four definitions in one sitting and including the source each time. A common error is to define ‘well-being’ using the WHO definition of health, or to use “illness” and “disease” as if they mean the same thing. The command word ‘Describe’ on a 2-mark question expects the core meaning plus one relevant detail; ‘Explain’ on a 3-mark question requires you to give a reason why the definition matters, using “because” or “therefore”.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Health (WHO, 1948): a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being — not merely the absence of disease or infirmity. A holistic, positive concept that covers three dimensions.
  • Illness (British Medical Journal): the personal, subjective feeling of being unwell. Can exist without disease; disease can exist without illness. The two do not always coincide.
  • Well-being (Psychology Today): being happy, healthy and thriving — with good mental health, high life satisfaction, a sense of purpose and the ability to manage stress. Varies across cultures, time and life stages.

practice_questions.text:
According to the WHO definition, health is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and:
A) The presence of all essential nutrients in the body
B) Not merely the absence of disease or infirmity
C) Freedom from stress and anxiety at all times
D) A high level of fitness and regular exercise
practice_questions.marks: B) Not merely the absence of disease or infirmity [1 mark]. This is the verbatim WHO definition from 1948. All other options are plausible but incorrect.

practice_questions.text: Identify the organisation responsible for the definition of health used in this qualification.
practice_questions.marks: The World Health Organization / WHO [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by 'illness' in health and social care.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for the core meaning (the personal / subjective feeling or experience of being unwell); 1 mark for a relevant qualifying detail (e.g. illness is personal to the individual and may not always match a medically identified disease; a person can experience illness without a diagnosable disease being present).

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between illness and disease, using an example to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for defining illness (the subjective personal experience of feeling unwell); 1 mark for defining disease (an objective clinical condition with specific identifiable signs and symptoms); 1 mark for an accurate example that illustrates the difference (e.g. a person may feel genuinely fatigued and unwell — illness — but medical tests find no identifiable condition — no disease present; or a person with early-stage hypertension has a diagnosed disease but feels completely well in themselves — disease without illness).

practice_questions.text: Discuss how the WHO definition of health is different from simply being free from illness or disease.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): Identifies that the WHO definition is holistic (covers physical, mental and social dimensions); explains that 'not merely the absence of disease' means health is a positive state, not just the lack of something negative; discusses what this means in practice for health promotion and care. May also explore the high bar set by 'complete' well-being and whether it is achievable. Uses developed reasoning with 'because', 'therefore'.

Secure (3–4 marks): Identifies the holistic nature and makes some comparison with 'just not being ill'; some development.

Developing (2 marks): Notes that health includes mental and social dimensions but does not fully develop the argument.

Emerging (1 mark): Quotes part of the definition without explanation.

practice_questions.text:
Nadia is 58 years old. She has been feeling exhausted, low in mood and unable to concentrate for several months. Her GP has run blood tests which have come back clear. Nadia feels that something is wrong but has been told she is 'medically fine.'

Using the definitions of health, illness and well-being, analyse how Nadia's situation demonstrates the complexity of assessing an individual's health and well-being.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): Applies all three definitions accurately to Nadia's circumstances. Illness — Nadia is clearly experiencing illness: the subjective feeling of being unwell is present (exhaustion, low mood, poor concentration); the fact that blood tests are clear does not mean illness is absent, because illness is personal and subjective [1+1]. Disease — no diagnosable disease has been found, which illustrates that illness can exist without disease [1]. Health — Nadia does not meet the WHO definition of complete physical, mental and social well-being: her mental well-being (mood, concentration) is affected, and social well-being may also be compromised if she is withdrawing from activities [1+1]. Well-being — Nadia is not thriving or experiencing high life satisfaction; her ability to manage stress and sense of purpose appear diminished [1]. Analysis chains the concepts: the complexity is that traditional clinical measures of health (blood tests) do not capture Nadia's subjective experience of illness or her reduced well-being; a holistic approach, as implied by the WHO definition, would take her experience seriously alongside the test results [1+1].

Secure (5–6 marks): Applies at least two definitions with mostly accurate analysis linked to Nadia.

Developing (3–4 marks): Applies one definition with limited reference to Nadia.

Emerging (1–2 marks): Names one definition with minimal application.

knowledge_checks.q: Which organisation provides the definition of health used in this qualification?
Which of the following is the best description of 'illness' in health and social care?
options: A clinically identified condition with specific signs and symptoms
The subjective, personal feeling or experience of being unwell
A complete state of physical, mental and social well-being
Being happy, healthy and thriving with high life satisfaction

knowledge_checks.q: The WHO defines health as a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the _____ of disease or infirmity.
The definition of well-being used in this qualification is drawn from _____ Today.
Match each concept to its authoritative source:

flashcard_questions.q: State the WHO definition of health.
flashcard_questions.a: A state of complete physical, mental and social well-being — not merely the absence of disease or infirmity.

flashcard_questions.q: Which organisation provides the definition of health used in this qualification?
What is 'illness' in health and social care?
flashcard_questions.a: The personal, subjective feeling or experience of being unwell, unique to the individual.

flashcard_questions.q: Which source is used for the definition of illness?
Give an example of illness existing without disease.
flashcard_questions.a: A person feeling fatigued and unwell but all medical tests returning clear.

flashcard_questions.q: What is 'disease' in health and social care?
flashcard_questions.a: A specific medical condition with identifiable signs (observable) and symptoms (reported by the patient).

flashcard_questions.q: What is the Psychology Today definition of well-being?
flashcard_questions.a: Being happy, healthy and thriving — with good mental health, high life satisfaction, a sense of purpose and ability to manage stress.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is the WHO definition of health described as 'holistic'?
flashcard_questions.a: It covers physical, mental and social dimensions — not just the physical body.

flashcard_questions.q: How can disease be present without illness?
flashcard_questions.a: A person may have an early-stage diagnosed condition but feel completely well in themselves.

flashcard_questions.q: In which three ways does understanding of health and well-being vary?
flashcard_questions.a: Across cultures, across time, and across life stages.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does the WHO definition say 'not merely the absence of disease'?
flashcard_questions.a: Because health is a positive state — freedom from disease alone is not enough to be healthy.

flashcard_questions.q: How does well-being differ from health?
flashcard_questions.a: Well-being emphasises subjective thriving and life satisfaction; health focuses on a complete positive state across three dimensions.

glossary_terms.definition: A United Nations agency responsible for public health, which provides internationally recognised definitions of health and well-being.
The personal feeling or subjective experience of being unwell, which is unique to the individual and may not always match a medically identified disease.
A specific medical condition with identifiable signs (observable by a practitioner) and symptoms (reported by the patient), which can typically be diagnosed and given a name.

A positive state of being that goes beyond the absence of illness, involving feeling happy, healthy and thriving, with good mental health, high life satisfaction, a sense of purpose, and the ability to manage stress.

items.title: What Makes a Good Life? | Robert Waldinger | TED
items.description: The director of the longest-running study on happiness explains what genuinely contributes to well-being — a compelling scientific perspective on the WHO's holistic definition.

items.title: How to Practise Emotional First Aid | Guy Winch | TED
items.description: Winch argues that we treat physical health more seriously than mental health — directly illustrating why the WHO's definition covers all three dimensions, not just the physical.

items.title: The Weight of the Nation (2012)
items.description: HBO documentary series on the US obesity epidemic — explores how disease, illness and well-being intersect and how personal and population health relate.

items.title: WHO — Constitution: Definition of Health
items.description: The official WHO text of the 1948 definition of health — primary source for the exam requirement to name the WHO and quote the definition accurately.

items.title: NHS — What Is Well-being?
items.description: NHS Every Mind Matters page on well-being — a UK public health perspective on what well-being means in practice.

items.title: Office for National Statistics — Measuring Well-being
items.description: The ONS national well-being framework and data dashboard — shows how well-being is measured at a population level beyond simple health statistics.

items.title: Mind — What Is Well-being?
items.description: Mind's plain-language explanation of well-being and the difference between mental health and ill mental health — useful for distinguishing the four key concepts.
